after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Express $z=\frac{10}{-3+4\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give $\theta $ in radians to three decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-3-4\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{10}{-3+4\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{10(-3-4\text{i})}{((-3)+4\text{i})((-3)-4\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{10(-3-4\text{i})}{(-3)^{2}-16{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-30-40\text{i}}{9+16} \\  & =-\frac{30}{25}-\frac{40}{25}\text{i} \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}-\frac{8}{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=-\frac{6}{5}-\frac{8}{5}\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{6}{5})}^{2}+{(-\frac{8}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{6}^{2}+{8}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{100}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=-\frac{6}{5}$ and $y=-\frac{8}{5}$ are both negative, $z$ lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{(-\frac{8}{5})}{(-\frac{6}{5})}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & ≈4.069,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4.069)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4.069))
$$

content.knowledge_point: Expressing a Quotient of Complex Numbers in Polar Form
content.problem: Express $z=\frac{10}{-3+4\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give $\theta $ in radians to three decimal places.
content.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-3-4\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{10}{-3+4\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{10(-3-4\text{i})}{((-3)+4\text{i})((-3)-4\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{10(-3-4\text{i})}{(-3)^{2}-16{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-30-40\text{i}}{9+16} \\  & =-\frac{30}{25}-\frac{40}{25}\text{i} \\  & =-\frac{6}{5}-\frac{8}{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=-\frac{6}{5}-\frac{8}{5}\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{6}{5})}^{2}+{(-\frac{8}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{6}^{2}+{8}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{100}{25}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=-\frac{6}{5}$ and $y=-\frac{8}{5}$ are both negative, $z$ lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{(-\frac{8}{5})}{(-\frac{6}{5})}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & ≈4.069,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4.069)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4.069))
$$

decision.explanation: The numerator and denominator both have magnitude 2, so r=1. Their arguments are π/3 and π/6, respectively, so the quotient has argument π/3−π/6=π/6. Thus option d is correct.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $\sqrt{3}-\text{i}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{1+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}}{\sqrt{3}+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{(1+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})(\sqrt{3}-\text{i})}{(\sqrt{3}+\text{i})(\sqrt{3}-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}+2\text{i}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(\sqrt{3}+\text{i})}{3+1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}+\text{i}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{\text{i}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{\text{i}}{2},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}$ are both positive, $z$ lies in the first quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})
$$

content.knowledge_point: Expressing a Quotient of Complex Numbers in Polar Form
content.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $\sqrt{3}-\text{i}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{1+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}}{\sqrt{3}+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{(1+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})(\sqrt{3}-\text{i})}{(\sqrt{3}+\text{i})(\sqrt{3}-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}+2\text{i}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(\sqrt{3}+\text{i})}{3+1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}+\text{i}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{\text{i}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\frac{\text{i}}{2},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}$ are both positive, $z$ lies in the first quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})
$$
